body.hook: Every great character wants something. Romeo wants Juliet. A villain wants power. Your character in a two-minute scene wants something too. Find what they want and what stands in their way, and you'll know how to play them.

study.title: What Do They Want?
study.question: How do traits, objectives and obstacles shape a character?
study.passage:
Scene (written for this lesson):
MAYA: (bursting in) You have to come with me. Now.
JORDAN: I'm in the middle of something.
MAYA: The tryout list is up. Your name's on it.
JORDAN: (not looking up) I didn't sign up.
MAYA: I signed you up.
JORDAN: You did what?
MAYA: You're the best player in our grade and you hide in here every lunch.
JORDAN: Maybe I like it in here.
MAYA: Nobody likes it in here. You're scared.
JORDAN: (long pause) What if I'm not good enough?
MAYA: Then at least you'll know.
Task: In pairs, read the scene twice. For each character, find: three traits (with evidence from lines), the objective (what they want), the obstacle (what stops them), and the motivation (why). Write a role profile, including details the script doesn't say (age, favourite food, a secret) that fit the evidence.

body.hook: Professional actors rarely nail a scene on the first try. They read it, block it, run it, get notes and run it again. Rehearsal isn't repeating; it's discovering something new each time.

study.title: Rehearsal Room
study.question: How does rehearsal turn a script into a performance?
study.passage:
Rehearsal process (written for this lesson), using the Maya and Jordan scene:
1. Read-through (5 minutes): Read the scene aloud, seated.
2. Beats (10 minutes): Divide the scene into beats. Mark a line wherever the tactic changes. Example: Beat 1, Maya commands ("You have to come with me"); Beat 2, Maya reveals the news; Beat 3, Maya confronts ("You're scared"); Beat 4, Jordan admits the truth.
3. Tactics (5 minutes): Give each beat an active tactic verb: to order, to tease, to challenge, to comfort, to avoid, to confess.
4. Run-through (5 minutes): Stand up and perform the whole scene.
5. Notes (10 minutes): Another pair watches and gives two notes using the language of objective and tactic: "Maya, try challenging instead of yelling in beat 3."
6. Second run (5 minutes): Apply the notes. What changed?
7. Memorization tip: learn the scene beat by beat, not line by line.

body.objective: Students will be able to stay in character under pressure.
body.iCan: I can stay in character under pressure.
successCriteria: I can stay in character when distracted
I can recover from mistakes without breaking
I can keep my objective going under pressure
body.hook: A phone rings in the audience. A prop falls. Your partner skips a line. The audience is watching to see if you'll break. Real actors stay in character no matter what, and that focus is a skill you can train.

study.title: Stay in the Scene
study.question: How do actors stay in character under pressure?
study.passage:
Activities (written for this lesson):
1. Focus game, Don't laugh (5 minutes): Partners face each other. One tries to make the other laugh without touching (faces, silly voices). The other stays neutral, breathing slowly and focusing on a spot on the partner's forehead.
2. Given circumstances (5 minutes): Before performing, each actor answers silently: Who am I? Where am I? What just happened before I entered? What do I want?
3. Distraction run (15 minutes): Perform your Maya and Jordan scene while the teacher adds distractions: a dropped book, a noise, a light flicker, an audience member coughing. Keep going.
4. Recovery drills (15 minutes): The teacher secretly tells one actor to skip a line or drop a prop. The partner must recover in character, for example by paraphrasing the missed information or using the dropped prop in the scene.
5. Debrief: What helped you stay focused?
